reasoning: Failure-driven edits were all kept, and merge_level 1 edits from both groups were treated as equal tier, with failure taking precedence on overlap. Success edit 'keep generic word in standard name' was dropped. It covers the same point as the failure edit on dropping type nouns and keeping them only when inseparable from the standard name. Its 'Ace Hardware' example could also contradict the failure substitution test. The success 'relative-based descriptors' bullet shared an anchor and theme with the failure 'He/his/she -> the person' bullet, so I folded it into that edit (support_count 2, kept as failure). The success media-pointer and code/abbreviation edit shared an anchor with the failure multi-part-definition edit. I re-anchored it after the 'NEVER answer ... Always output the specific entity' sentence in Rule 1, where it fits semantically, so that no two edits target the same text. The remaining success edits (definition/etymology/alias headwords, game-board and lyric clues) cover patterns the failure edits don't and have unique anchors, so they are kept unchanged.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content:
- Default to the singular, bare headword, even when the clue says 'these' or 'one of these' ('these destructive sea waves' -> 'Tsunami', not 'tsunamis'; 'Well', not 'wells'). Use the plural only for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas'), for things whose standard name is plural ('Giblets'), or when a verbatim archive/flashcard hit shows the plural.
- 'This fruit / vegetable / grain' that a festival, harvest or industry is built around takes the plural form the passages use ('Strawberries', not 'strawberry'). 'These animals / plants / people' wants ONE bare noun for the best-supported member that the passages put first or most often ('Sheep'). Never write 'X or Y', and never add the body part or product from the passages ('sheep or goat intestines' is wrong).

edits.target: do not append that role word to the answer.
edits.content:
- Drop the generic type noun that the clue's 'this X' phrase already supplies, and drop corporate or descriptive suffixes. 'This island off North Carolina' -> 'Roanoke', not 'Roanoke Island'. 'This satellite radio company' -> 'Sirius', not 'Sirius Satellite Radio'. 'This river / lake / city / company / team' -> the bare name. Keep the type word only when it is inseparable from the standard name ('Hundred Years' War', 'World War II', 'Swiss cheese' for an alias clue). Test: put your answer in place of 'this X' in the clue. If a word is now repeated ('island ... Roanoke Island'), delete it.
- For people, use the plain 'First Last' form by which the person is commonly known, without middle names, initials or suffixes ('George Bush', not 'George H. W. Bush'). If the clue itself names the same person in some form, copy that form. A name form in a verbatim archive hit overrides this.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- SUBSTITUTION TEST: put your candidate in place of 'this X / these X / it' and reread the clue. The answer must be a member of the category X names (this season -> Fall/Winter/Spring/Summer; this island -> an island; these creatures -> a kind of creature). It must NOT be a phrase copied from the clue (a dish, a company, an event) or a word from the clue's own descriptors ('strange creatures'). Never answer with the clue's subject. The clue states a fact about the subject and asks for the thing the fact is tied to.
- '<Acronym or name> stands for ...' or 'short for ...' asks for the full expansion of the letters ('Digimon' -> 'Digital Monsters'). Give the expansion's words, not a descriptor from the clue. If a passage glosses the name ('Digimon: Digital Monsters'), copy that gloss.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content:
- Part vs whole: 'one of the buildings / rooms / towers at this site is named for X', 'a wing of this museum', or 'a gate of this city' asks for the WHOLE place that contains the named part ('Tower of London'), never the part itself ('Devereux Tower'). Passages that mention the part inside the larger place's page give the answer.
- Plain definition clues ('A short, witty saying', 'a crime for which ...', 'part of a racetrack ...') want the single dictionary term the definition fits best. Choose the headword whose definition matches ALL the clue's key words (short + witty + saying -> 'Epigram', whose entry reads 'a witty, ingenious, or pointed saying tersely expressed'), not a looser synonym ('quip'). Prefer the term whose dictionary/thesaurus/crossword snippet in the context nearly repeats the clue's wording.

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content: - Multi-part definition clues ('Aussie slang for a pub, it's also a shack; poor people may live in a "town" of them') want ONE word that satisfies EVERY part ('shanty': a shack, Aussie slang for a pub, 'shanty town'). Test each candidate against each part. A quoted word such as 'town' is often the second half of a compound, so answer the first half. Never answer with a descriptive word lifted from the clue ('poor'). If the passages are noisy or the archive snippet is cut off before the answer, use your own vocabulary knowledge.

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content:
- 'He / his / she' in a clue that names a work, slogan, quote or event ('between 2 more famous pictures, he worked on his "Virgin and Child with St. Anne"') asks for the PERSON, never the works or titles the passages list ('Leonardo da Vinci', not 'The Last Supper, Mona Lisa'). A slogan or pair clue that names one of two people ('Tippecanoe and Tyler too', 'Lemmon & this actor') wants the OTHER person ('William Henry Harrison'). Do not answer with both names or with the one already given. Always give exactly one entity, never a list.
- Relative-based descriptors ('his grandfather, the adding machine inventor, ...', 'her sister, the actress ...') describe a relative. The answer is the person the clue is about (the 'he' or 'she' of the sentence, here the author of "Naked Lunch"), not the relative. Pick the name that the passages tie to ALL the clue's details.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content:
- 'This organization's / league's / city's X' (Hall of Fame, team, building): answer the OWNER ('LPGA'), not the X ('World Golf Hall of Fame'). If your answer repeats the clue's own noun phrase ('Hall of Fame'), it fills the wrong slot.
- Role clues ('GOP leader', 'chief', 'founder', 'champion') need someone who actually held that role. Do not pick a name because a generic phrase from the clue ('first and foremost') sits next to it in one snippet, or because he currently holds a related office (a sitting senator). Clues are often years old. Choose the person the passages tie to the role (e.g. a headline like 'Sen. Trent Lott gives up Senate GOP leader's post') and to every other detail, such as the state.

edits.target: Always output the specific entity, word, or name that the clue is asking for.
edits.content:
- Pointers to unseen media ('the dipper seen here', 'this instrument heard here', 'shown here', 'this picture') and stage-direction parentheticals ('(Jimmy of the Clue Crew ...)') are not part of the fact. Ignore them and answer from the remaining textual descriptors plus the entity the passages tie to them ('used with this sticky substance' -> honey; 'handheld percussion instrument a minstrel could use' -> tambourine). Never reply that the image, video or audio is missing.
- A code, abbreviation or initialism in the clue ('Let freedom ring: PHL', 'MSY', 'Ga.', 'NYSE') stands for a full entity. Decode it (PHL = Philadelphia's airport) and answer with the full place or name that matches the rest of the clue. Use the passages to confirm the decoding (here, Liberty Bell and Independence Hall passages).

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Definition, etymology, synonym and alias clues ('From the Middle Dutch for "little barrel", it's another way of saying yokel', 'Americans refer to Emmentaler as this', 'sickle-shaped weapon of the Aborigines'): find the dictionary or reference snippet that restates the clue's key phrase and answer with the term it defines (the headword, e.g. 'bumpkin', 'Boomerang') or the alternate name it gives ('Swiss cheese'). Do not answer with a word from inside the definition (yokel, hayseed, sickle).

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content:
- A game-board or recap page (e.g. 'JEOPARDY! Game - <date>') may repeat the clue with no answer. Treat it as confirmation that the clue is genuine. Take the answer from the other passages that match the clue's specific facts (year, place, event), plus your own knowledge ('dying on a plane en route to a Houston hospital in 1976' -> Howard Hughes).
- Lyric clues ('1991 hit that contains the lines "..."') want the song title. Look for passages where the lyric line sits next to a title, and give the bare title without quotation marks.
